questions.q: When a panel asks why Meridian doesn't just give each hospital system its own instance, what is the core of the correct defense?
options: Each hospital system should actually get its own instance, and the panel's challenge reveals a flaw in the design
Historical autonomy is, by itself, a sufficient technical justification for a second production instance
Instances are free to add in ServiceNow, so the question has no real cost implication

Meridian has neither of Chapter 2's legitimate justifications for a second instance, and the real autonomy concern is a governance problem better solved by Lesson 29's federated governance model than by multiplying instances
questions.explain: The strong defense names the real test from Chapter 2, shows Meridian fails it, and redirects the real political concern to the governance fix already identified in Lesson 29.

questions.q: What is the honest answer to 'how does this scale if a fourth hospital system joins in two years'?
options: Domain Separation scales infinitely with zero added cost regardless of how many domains are added
A fourth hospital system would require abandoning Domain Separation entirely and rebuilding from scratch
This scenario was never considered and has no real answer

Adding a domain is a bounded, known pattern that scales better than adding a full instance, but it's not free — each added domain compounds the domain-aware testing overhead, which should be periodically reconsidered
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly avoids overselling the design — it names the real, compounding cost of each additional domain rather than claiming the approach scales for free.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say defaulting to event-driven integration 'for consistency' would be the wrong answer to the request-response challenge?
options: Chapter 4 holds that neither pattern is categorically better — the HR rep waiting on a case screen needs an immediate answer, which is exactly what request-response is for, and forcing event-driven there adds unneeded complexity
Event-driven integration is technically impossible to implement for HR data
Consistency across integration patterns is always the correct architectural goal regardless of context
Request-response was chosen purely because it was easier to build, with no real justification
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly rejects 'consistency for its own sake' and reaffirms Chapter 4's actual decision criteria: match the pattern to the real need.

questions.q: How does the lesson defend the security design against the claim that light controls on most of the platform are a compliance risk?
options: The design should be changed on the spot to lock down the entire platform uniformly
Compliance risk is not a real concern for a Technical Architect to consider

Uniform maximum restriction produces worse real security outcomes (shared logins, shadow spreadsheets), so controls are deliberately concentrated on the regulated zone while staying low-friction elsewhere to keep work inside the governed platform
Light controls everywhere are always acceptable regardless of what data is involved
questions.explain: The correct defense holds the line using Chapter 5's reasoning rather than overcorrecting into uniform restriction under pressure.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real skill this entire capstone has been building, beyond the diagrams and documents produced?
options: Producing the most visually polished architecture diagrams possible
Avoiding ever changing a position once it has been stated to a panel
Memorizing a fixed script of answers to repeat verbatim regardless of the questions asked

The underlying judgment to weigh real constraints, name honest tradeoffs, and hold a reasoned position under live challenge — the same judgment tested in real client engagements and the real CTA assessment
questions.explain: The lesson closes by naming judgment under pressure, not the artifacts themselves, as the transferable skill this capstone practiced.
